title: Dog bite or other animal bite
summary: Animal bites carry infection risk and, depending on the animal and region, the risk of rabies. Wound care plus medical review is the rule, not the exception.
steps: Move away from the animal to a safe place.
Wash the wound thoroughly with running water and soap for at least 15 minutes. This single step removes most rabies virus.
After washing, apply an antiseptic if available (povidone iodine or alcohol-based).
Press a clean cloth on the wound if it is still bleeding.
Cover the wound loosely with a clean dressing.
Note the type of animal, whether it was a pet or stray, whether the bite was provoked, and whether the animal is vaccinated and available for observation.
Get to a clinic or hospital the same day for a tetanus check and a rabies risk assessment.
avoid: Do not skip washing the wound — it is the most important first step against rabies.
Do not stitch the wound closed yourself.
Do not apply turmeric, ash, chillies, or other home pastes inside the wound.
Do not delay rabies post-exposure care while you 'wait and see' — the vaccine works only if started early.
Do not put yourself or others at risk to capture or kill the animal.
whenToEscalate: Always — see a doctor the same day for tetanus and rabies risk assessment.
Emergency immediately for: deep or wide wounds, bites to the face, hands, or genitals, heavy bleeding, signs of nerve or tendon damage, or any bite from a wild, sick, or behaving-strangely animal.
Bites in children, elderly people, or pregnant people — extra urgent.
Any developing redness, warmth, pus, fever, or red streaks spreading from the wound in the days afterward.
specialty: Emergency department or rabies post-exposure clinic; general physician for tetanus update.
